newsitem.title: BOSNIA: IMF says Bosnia deal possible by mid-July.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Bosnia deal possible by mid-July.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Monday it hoped to reach a stand-by agreement with Bosnia in time for a fund-raising conference set for mid-July.
Bosnia's peacetime government bowed to international pressure last week and endorsed a package of economic laws prescribed by foreign experts, paving the way for an historic agreement with the IMF.

"The first requirement -- the passage of the state economic laws -- has now been met and discussion will continue on the remaining issues during the next two weeks," Scott Brown, IMF chief of mission in Bosnia, told reporters.

Since late last year, the IMF has sought to forge an agreement with Bosnian authorities on an economic programme that would be supported by a stand-by agreement and $100 million in assistance over a one year period, Brown said.

But political bickering prevented adoption of the legislation for months. Only the threat of cancelling a reconstruction aid conference prompted Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders to adopt the package last Friday.
The adoption of the legislation came too late for the donors' conference which was set for June 24 in Brussels and had to be moved until mid-July, pending an agreement with the IMF.

The IMF still wants to see an agreement on the design of the new joint currency and initial steps made to carry out the country's budget and central bank laws before signing a letter of intent with Bosnia, Brown said.
"We'll certainly do everything we can (to have a letter of intent before the donors' conference) but I don't try to predict any more," he said.

Experts say the importance of Bosnia's agreement with the IMF goes beyond the $100 million in aid and will certify that the country is pursuing a market-oriented course which will reassure foreign donors, direct investors and creditors.
"Most external creditors regard an agreement with the IMF as a precondition for finishing negotiations to reduce and reschedule external debt," Brown said.
"This is certainly true of the Paris Club...and as a matter of practice the commercial banks in the London Club usually wait for an IMF agreement to finalise agreements," he said.

Bosnia inherited a $3.5 billion debt as one of the former Yugoslav republics, according to a World Bank study. Of that, $2 billion is in arrears and the country plans to start debt restructuring negotiations as soon as possible.
Brown said discussions on technical issues were probably already under way between creditors and Bosnian authorities to prepare the way for negotiations after the IMF programme is in place.
"Whenever this IMF arrangement is agreed upon and approved by the (IMF) board, that would be the point at which the real show could begin with the London and Paris clubs," he said.
